opus-5.5.text:
I think for me the appeal was never really about leaving physics. It felt more like carrying physics with me into a new territory.

When I was an undergrad doing physics, I was trained to ask a certain kind of question: what are the underlying principles, what's the simplest model that captures the phenomenon, can we find something like a conservation law or a symmetry that explains why things behave the way they do? And then I looked at AI, especially deep learning, and it struck me that it's this enormous, very successful empirical field, and yet in many ways we don't understand why it works. It's a bit like physics before Newton. Lots of observations, lots of engineering tricks, but not many "laws."

That gap is very exciting for a young researcher. In mature areas of physics, many of the big questions have been worked on by brilliant people for a century, and the low-hanging fruit is mostly gone. In AI, you can still find phenomena nobody has explained, like grokking, or scaling laws, or why certain representations emerge, and you can attack them with fairly simple tools: toy models, careful experiments, some intuition from statistical physics or dynamical systems. A single student with a laptop can still discover something genuinely new. That's a rare situation in science.

There's also a second direction I care about, which is not only physics for AI, but AI for physics. If we build models that are more interpretable, like the work we've done on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, the hope is that AI becomes a tool scientists can actually talk to, where it helps you rediscover formulas or symmetries rather than just giving you a black-box prediction. So for me the two directions form a loop: physics helps us understand AI, and understandable AI helps us do better physics.

And honestly, part of the appeal is just the speed. In AI, ideas move very fast and the feedback loop is short. You can have an idea in the morning and run an experiment by the evening. For someone young and curious, that tempo is addictive. The challenge is to keep the physicist's patience and taste for deep understanding while living in such a fast-moving field. I think that tension is actually where a lot of interesting work comes from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI has unexplained phenomena a student can investigate and that mature physics has fewer open opportunities, but it does not identify high-energy physics specifically as the comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that physics, especially the kind of fundamental physics I grew up admiring, has become a place where progress is slow and the big questions are very far away. When I was an undergraduate in physics at Peking University, I had this romantic picture of discovering new laws of nature. But the reality is that the low-hanging fruit in theoretical physics was mostly picked in the twentieth century, and today a young person can spend an entire career on a very narrow problem without seeing a clear result.

AI felt like the opposite. It's a field where the fundamentals are not understood at all. We have these neural networks that work incredibly well, and nobody really knows why. That's exactly the situation a physicist dreams of: lots of phenomena, lots of experimental data, and almost no theory. It reminded me of thermodynamics before statistical mechanics, or electricity and magnetism before Maxwell. There's a sense that the laws are waiting to be found, and that the tools of physics, like thinking about symmetry, conservation, scaling, and phase transitions, actually have something to say.

So for me the appeal was partly intellectual and partly about timing. You get to be an early explorer. You can run an experiment on a laptop in an afternoon and see something nobody has seen before. In particle physics you might wait ten years for the collider to produce data. In AI the feedback loop is days or hours. For a young researcher that pace is intoxicating.

There is also a deeper motivation, which is that I never wanted to leave physics behind. My hope is that going into AI is a way of coming back to physics with new tools. If we can build models that are interpretable, that can discover equations and structure on their own, then AI becomes an instrument for science, not just a technology. Work like KAN, the Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, came out of that mindset: can we design architectures that are not only accurate but also legible to a scientist, so that a human and a machine can collaborate on understanding?

And I should say, there's a human side too. The AI community is young, open, and fast. People share code, share ideas, argue on Twitter. Coming from a more traditional academic culture, that openness felt very freeing. You don't have to wait for permission to try something.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI as an unexplored field where a young researcher can be an early explorer, contrasting its fast feedback with particle physics, where data may take ten years. This communicates the perception that AI offers more research opportunities as a reason for the move.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal is that AI gives you a new way to ask some of the questions that make physics exciting. How does complex behavior emerge from simple rules? Can we find a simple explanation underneath something that looks very complicated?

In physics, you learn to look for structure, build simplified models, and test your intuition. Those habits are useful in AI, too. You can build a system, run an experiment, and discover that your explanation was wrong. That feedback can be very exciting for a young researcher.

But I don’t think of it as simply leaving physics behind. It can be a way to bring a physicist’s curiosity into a new setting—and perhaps develop tools that eventually help us understand physics better.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as a new setting for physics questions and says the research feedback is exciting, but it does not identify greater research opportunities in AI than in high-energy physics as the reason for moving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal is that you can bring a physicist’s way of thinking to a field where there are still many basic questions to ask. In physics, you learn to look for simple principles behind complicated behavior. With AI, you can ask: What is the system actually learning? Why does it generalize? Can we find a simpler description of what’s happening inside?

For a young researcher, that’s exciting because you can move between an idea and an experiment relatively quickly. You propose an explanation, test it, and let the result challenge your intuition. And AI can also become a tool for doing science, so moving into it doesn’t necessarily mean leaving your interest in physics behind.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as exciting because it has basic questions to explore and allows quick experiments, but it does not say AI offers more research opportunities than high-energy physics.
